nodes.text: Unit 2B Hub: Applications of Derivatives

Unit 2A taught how derivatives are defined and computed. Unit 2B turns those calculations into information and decisions. The central question is no longer merely ``what is the derivative?'' but ``what does this derivative let us conclude?''

children.text: [title={The practical meaning}] A derivative is useful when its sign, size, units, or zeros answer a real question. Positive or negative may describe direction. A zero may identify a candidate peak. A second derivative may show whether growth is speeding up or slowing down. A tangent line may replace a difficult function near one convenient input.

nodes.text: Main sequence

\item Interpretation, higher derivatives, motion, and rates from data. \item Local linearity, differentials, uncertainty, and Newton's method. \item Related rates and geometric modeling. \item Extrema, the Mean Value Theorem, increasing/decreasing behavior, concavity, and curve analysis. \item Optimization in geometry, science, engineering, and business. \item L'Hopital's Rule and indeterminate forms. \item Modeling studios, advanced notes, cumulative review, and exams.

Before beginning, calculate or explain each item.

children.text: Differentiate \(x^4-3x^2+1\).
Differentiate \((x^2+1)^5\).
By the chain rule, \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2+1)^5=\boxed{10x(x^2+1)^4}\).
Differentiate \(x^2e^x\).
By the product rule, \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2e^x)=\boxed{e^x(x^2+2x)}\).
Find \(dy/dx\) for \(x^2+y^2=25\).
Differentiate implicitly: \(2x+2yy'=0\), so \(\boxed{dy/dx=-x/y}\) where \(y\ne0\).
State the units of \(C'(q)\) if \(C\) is dollars and \(q\) is items.
Because cost is measured in dollars and output in items, \(C'(q)\) is measured in \(\boxed{\text{dollars per item}}\).
Divide by 3 and factor: \(x^2-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3)=0\), so \(\boxed{x=1,3}\).
Explain why a solution of \(f'(x)=0\) is only a candidate for an extremum.

The equation \(f'(x)=0\) only identifies a stationary candidate. A sign change, comparison of values, or another valid test is still needed; for example, \(f(x)=x^3\) has \(f'(0)=0\) but no extremum at 0.

children.text: Turn a verbal situation into variables, equations, derivatives, and a contextual conclusion.

nodes.text: A Reliable Translation Process

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] The model in \emph{How to Translate Derivative Word Problems} is a simplified mathematical description, not reality itself. Begin by identifying inputs, outputs, units, assumptions, and the range over which the formula is intended to be credible. The derivative then measures sensitivity inside that model.

Interpret both the amount and its rate. A peak may occur where the derivative is zero, but a decision based on that peak must still respect constraints and model limitations. Strong applied work includes a reasonableness check and says what the calculation does not establish.

nodes.title: A word problem is a model-building problem before it is a calculus problem

children.text: [title={A word problem is a model-building problem before it is a calculus problem}] The derivative is rarely the first line of work. Begin by naming the quantities, assigning units, and deciding which variable depends on which. Draw a diagram when geometry is involved. Write one equation that expresses the relationship, and only then differentiate.

The final sentence matters as much as the derivative. It should identify the quantity changing, the input with respect to which it changes, the instant or state being considered, the sign, and the units. This translation is what turns a correct calculation into an answer to the actual question.

nodes.text: A word problem is not a decorative version of a formula exercise. It asks you to build the mathematical object before using it. That is why students can know every derivative rule and still feel stuck when a ladder slides, a balloon rises, or a company changes production.
Use the following translation process.

\item \textbf{Name the variables.} Include units and identify which variable depends on which. \item \textbf{Write what is known.} Separate constant values from rates such as \(dx/dt\). \item \textbf{Build one governing relationship.} Use geometry, a physical law, or a stated model. \item \textbf{Differentiate before inserting the changing snapshot.} The relationship must remain valid while the quantities change. \item \textbf{Substitute the instant-specific values.} \item \textbf{Solve for the requested rate or quantity.} \item \textbf{Interpret the sign, units, and size.}

children.text: Compute and interpret second and higher derivatives.

nodes.text: Interpreting Higher Derivatives, Motion, and Change
From Computation to Interpretation

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] The graphs in \emph{Higher Derivatives} should be read vertically through a common input. A height on the derivative graph is a slope on the original graph. A zero of velocity is a horizontal tangent of position; a zero of acceleration is a horizontal tangent of velocity.

Do not match graphs by superficial shape. Translate one feature at a time: sign, zeros, increasing behavior, and concavity. This produces a defensible interpretation even when the graphs are unfamiliar or not drawn to a convenient scale.

[title={Rates have their own rates}] A positive first derivative means an amount is increasing; it does not tell you whether that increase is speeding up or slowing down. The second derivative answers that second question by measuring change in the first derivative.

Keep the levels separate. In motion, position can be decreasing while acceleration is positive. In economics, cost can be rising while marginal cost is falling. The signs refer to different layers of behavior.

nodes.text: A derivative is itself a function, so it can be differentiated again. The second derivative measures how the first derivative changes, the third measures how the second changes, and so on. These layers encode acceleration, changing curvature, changing growth rates, and the shape of local approximations.

Higher derivatives are meaningful only when the required differentiability exists. A function may have a first derivative without having a second, so the notation \(f^{(n)}\) quietly carries a regularity assumption.

[title={Second derivative as changing slope}] If \(f''(a)>0\), then slopes of \(f\) are increasing near \(a\). If \(f''(a)<0\), slopes are decreasing. This is the foundation of concavity, developed later.

[title={Jerk and elevator comfort}] If an elevator's position is \(s(t)\), then \(s'\) is velocity, \(s''\) acceleration, and \(s^{(3)}\) jerk. Passengers notice abrupt changes in acceleration even when the acceleration itself remains within safe limits. Motion-control systems therefore smooth jerk as well as speed and acceleration. Higher derivatives can measure physically distinct layers of change.

nodes.title: Smooth does not always mean analytic

children.text: [title={Smooth does not always mean analytic}] A function may possess derivatives of every order and still fail to equal its Taylor series. The classic example

has every derivative equal to zero at the origin, so its Taylor series there is identically zero, while the function is positive away from zero. Later analysis distinguishes infinitely differentiable functions from analytic functions.

nodes.text: Sign, Size, Units, and the Reference Point

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] In \emph{How to Interpret a Derivative in Context}, separate the amount from its rate and the rate from its rate of change. Position, velocity, and acceleration may be evaluated at the same time, but they answer different questions and carry different units. A negative value describes direction or signed change; it does not automatically mean the quantity is small or slowing.

When reading a context, write a sentence for each derivative before calculating. Include what changes, with respect to what, at which input, and in what units. Then use signs to describe direction and compare signs of velocity and acceleration to determine whether speed is increasing or decreasing.

nodes.title: Read a derivative through units, sign, and scale

children.text: [title={Read a derivative through units, sign, and scale}] A derivative value is a compact sentence. Its units say what is changing per unit of what. Its sign says whether the output rises or falls as the input increases. Its magnitude says how sensitive the output is near that state.

For a small input change \(\Delta x\), the derivative also predicts \(\Delta f\approx f'(x)\Delta x\). That approximation gives the derivative operational meaning: it estimates what a nearby real change will do.

nodes.text: A derivative value is incomplete until four pieces are identified: the input where it is evaluated, the sign, the units, and the practical meaning of a small input change near that point.
Suppose \(P(t)\) is a population in thousands of people and \(t\) is years after 2020. The statement

means that at the start of 2026, population is increasing at an instantaneous rate of about \(1.8\) thousand people per year. It also predicts that a small time increase \(\Delta t\) near that moment produces
thousand people.

children.text: [title={A complete interpretation template}] At input \(x=a\), the quantity \(f\) is [increasing/decreasing] at approximately \(|f'(a)|\) [output units per input unit]. Therefore, for a small input change \(\Delta x\) near \(a\), the output changes by approximately \(f'(a)\Delta x\).
If \(T'(12)=-0.4\) and \(T\) is degrees Celsius while time is minutes, give a complete interpretation.
At \(t=12\) minutes, the temperature is decreasing at about \(0.4\) degrees Celsius per minute.

children.text: Translate among position, velocity, acceleration, and speed.

nodes.text: One-Dimensional Motion

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] Applied derivative values in \emph{Position, Velocity, and Acceleration} need interpretation, not just calculation. The number, sign, units, and scale all matter. A derivative of $4$ could mean four dollars per item, four meters per second, or four degrees per meter; those are completely different claims.

When data rather than a formula are given, state that the derivative is estimated. Identify the finite difference used, preserve the units, and report precision consistent with the measurements. More decimal places do not create more information.

nodes.title: Motion uses three related graphs, not one interchangeable picture

children.text: [title={Motion uses three related graphs, not one interchangeable picture}] Position tells where the object is, velocity tells how position is changing, and acceleration tells how velocity is changing. A positive position does not imply positive velocity, and a negative velocity does not imply negative acceleration.

When reading a motion problem, ask one question at a time: where is the object, which direction is it moving, how fast is it moving, and is its velocity becoming more positive or more negative? The derivative relationships connect the answers without collapsing them into one number.

nodes.text: In one-dimensional motion, position tells where an object is, velocity tells how position changes, and acceleration tells how velocity changes. These are related functions, not interchangeable labels. In particular, velocity can be zero while acceleration is not, as at the top of a vertical toss.

Signs describe direction relative to the chosen coordinate axis. A negative velocity is not ``bad'' and a positive acceleration does not necessarily mean speeding up. Interpretation requires comparing both signs.

children.text: Determine when a particle speeds up or slows down.

nodes.text: Compare the Signs of Velocity and Acceleration

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] The graphs in \emph{Speeding Up and Slowing Down} should be read vertically through a common input. A height on the derivative graph is a slope on the original graph. A zero of velocity is a horizontal tangent of position; a zero of acceleration is a horizontal tangent of velocity.

Do not match graphs by superficial shape. Translate one feature at a time: sign, zeros, increasing behavior, and concavity. This produces a defensible interpretation even when the graphs are unfamiliar or not drawn to a convenient scale.

nodes.title: Speed changes according to whether velocity and acceleration cooperate

children.text: [title={Speed changes according to whether velocity and acceleration cooperate}] Speed is \(|v|\), so it increases when acceleration pushes velocity farther from zero. That occurs when velocity and acceleration have the same sign. Speed decreases when acceleration pushes velocity toward zero, which occurs when their signs differ.

A sign chart is safer than verbal intuition here. Negative velocity means motion in the negative direction, not automatically slowing down. An object with \(v<0\) and \(a<0\) is moving left faster and faster.

nodes.text: Speed is the magnitude \(|v|\), so an object speeds up when velocity moves away from zero and slows down when velocity moves toward zero. The clean sign test follows: velocity and acceleration with the same sign imply speeding up; opposite signs imply slowing down.

This is easier to understand on a number line than through memorization. Acceleration points in the direction that velocity is being pushed. If that push reinforces the current direction, speed grows; if it opposes the current direction, speed shrinks.

nodes.text: Translate Shape into Derivative Information

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] The graphs in \emph{Reading Function and Derivative Graphs} should be read vertically through a common input. A height on the derivative graph is a slope on the original graph. A zero of velocity is a horizontal tangent of position; a zero of acceleration is a horizontal tangent of velocity.

Do not match graphs by superficial shape. Translate one feature at a time: sign, zeros, increasing behavior, and concavity. This produces a defensible interpretation even when the graphs are unfamiliar or not drawn to a convenient scale.

nodes.title: Translate heights on one graph into slopes on another

children.text: [title={Translate heights on one graph into slopes on another}] To sketch \(f'\) from \(f\), begin where the slope information is clearest. Horizontal tangents on \(f\) become zeros of \(f'\). Rising intervals become positive regions; falling intervals become negative regions. Steeper parts of \(f\) produce larger magnitudes on \(f'\).
Do not copy the shape of \(f\). The derivative graph records slope, not height. A high point on \(f\) can correspond to a zero on \(f'\), and a low point on \(f\) can do the same.

nodes.text: Graph translation is a language skill. A rising original graph corresponds to a positive derivative; a local maximum corresponds to a derivative that changes from positive to negative; and a straight segment corresponds to a constant derivative. The derivative graph should be constructed from slopes, not from the heights of the original graph.

Read from both directions. Given \(f\), infer \(f'\); given \(f'\), reconstruct possible behavior of \(f\). The second task is less unique because many original functions can share the same derivative up to a vertical shift.
For a graph of \(f\):

\item \(f'>0\) where \(f\) increases; \item \(f'<0\) where \(f\) decreases; \item \(f'=0\) at horizontal tangents; \item large \(|f'|\) means a steep graph; \item \(f''>0\) where slopes are increasing; \item \(f''<0\) where slopes are decreasing.

nodes.title: Read a derivative graph as motion

children.text: [title={Read a derivative graph as motion}] Suppose \(s'(t)=v(t)\) is positive on \((0,2)\), zero at \(2\), negative on \((2,5)\), and increasing throughout. Describe \(s\).

Because \(v>0\), position increases on \((0,2)\). Because \(v<0\), position decreases on \((2,5)\). The particle changes direction at \(t=2\). Since \(v\) is increasing, \(s''=v'>0\), so the position graph is concave up throughout. A concave-up graph can still decrease; it simply decreases with slopes that become less negative.

nodes.title: Data give approximations whose quality depends on spacing and noise

children.text: [title={Data give approximations whose quality depends on spacing and noise}] A table cannot directly display an instantaneous rate because its rows are separated by finite intervals. Forward, backward, and central differences estimate the derivative by nearby secant slopes. Central differences are often more balanced because they use information on both sides.

Smaller spacing is not automatically better when measurements are noisy. Differentiation magnifies small fluctuations, so a responsible estimate reports the data interval and treats the result as approximate.

nodes.text: A table records finite differences, not exact instantaneous rates. Central differences often improve an estimate by using data on both sides of the target point, but every estimate inherits measurement error and spacing limitations from the data.

Context determines whether the number is plausible. A derivative of temperature with respect to time has different units and meaning from a derivative of temperature with respect to depth. Writing the units forces you to identify which relationship the data actually describes.
Suppose \(T(t)\) is temperature. Then \(T'\) measures temperature change per unit time. The second derivative \(T''\) measures how the warming or cooling rate itself changes.

children.text: Velocity gives direction; speed is \(|v|\). Speed increases when \(v\) and \(a\) share a sign. The second derivative measures the change of the first derivative and controls concavity.

A company's revenue \(R(q)\) has \(R'(100)=80\) and \(R''(100)=-0.6\). Interpret both values.

nodes.text: Linear Approximation, Differentials, and Newton's Method
A Smooth Curve Looks Like Its Tangent Up Close

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] The approximation in \emph{Local Linearity} replaces a nonlinear function with its best local line. The known value supplies the starting height, and the derivative supplies the rate of change. The estimate is useful because lines are easy to calculate with, not because the original curve has become exactly linear.

Always identify the center $a$ and the target $x$. Write $\Delta x=x-a$, calculate the predicted change $f'(a)\Delta x$, and then add it to $f(a)$. Use concavity or a numerical comparison to understand the direction and size of the error.

nodes.title: A differentiable curve has a best local line

children.text: [title={A differentiable curve has a best local line}] The tangent line is not merely a line that touches the graph. Near the contact point, it reproduces the function's value and first-order change. As you zoom in, the remaining difference between curve and line becomes small compared with the horizontal displacement.

This is why derivatives support approximation. Instead of evaluating a difficult function exactly at a nearby input, evaluate the tangent line, whose arithmetic is simple. The approximation is local, so distance from the base point matters.

nodes.text: A differentiable curve resembles a line when viewed closely enough. This is not merely a visual curiosity; it is the operational meaning of differentiability. The tangent line captures the function's first-order response to a small input change.

Local linearity explains why derivatives are useful even when exact formulas are complicated. Near a known input, the function can be replaced temporarily by a much simpler line, with an error that becomes relatively smaller as the input change shrinks.

nodes.text: Zooming In Turns Smooth Curves into Lines

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] Newton's method in \emph{Why a Tangent Line Can Approximate a Curve} repeatedly uses local linearity to solve a nonlinear equation. Each tangent line supplies an easier zero, which becomes the next estimate. The method can be spectacularly fast near a suitable root and unreliable from a poor starting point.

Record the iteration formula and a table of estimates. Check the function value as well as the digits of $x_n$. A sequence that appears stable on a calculator display may still have converged to the wrong root, entered a cycle, or encountered a nearly horizontal tangent.

nodes.title: Zooming is a mathematical test, not just a picture trick

children.text: [title={Zooming is a mathematical test, not just a picture trick}] A smooth graph looks straighter under magnification because its nonlinear error shrinks faster than the input change. The derivative is the slope of the line that survives this zooming process.

The phrase ``nearby'' cannot be removed. A tangent line may be excellent over a small interval and terrible far away. Every linear approximation should name its center and give some reason the target input is close enough.

nodes.text: A smooth curve is not globally a line, but near one point it becomes difficult to distinguish from its tangent line. Differentiability is exactly the condition that the linear error becomes small compared with the input change.
The approximation

does not claim that the curve and tangent are identical. It claims that the tangent captures the first-order change near \(a\). The approximation improves as \(\Delta x\) shrinks, unless numerical or measurement limitations become dominant.

An oil slick remains circular and area grows at \(100\) m\(^2\)/min. Find \(dr/dt\) at \(r=20\).

nodes.text: The first derivative test classifies a critical point by observing what the function does on either side. A change from increasing to decreasing produces a local maximum; decreasing to increasing produces a local minimum; no sign change produces neither.

children.text: Critical numbers locate candidates. The closed interval method finds absolute extrema. Rolle's and Mean Value Theorems guarantee interior derivative behavior under continuity and differentiability hypotheses. Signs of \(f'\) determine monotonicity; signs of \(f''\) determine concavity.
Find absolute extrema of \(x^4-4x^2\) on \([-3,2]\).

\(f'(x)=4x(x^2-2)\), so candidates are \(-3,-\sqrt2,0,\sqrt2,2\). Their values are \(45,-4,0,-4,0\). Therefore the absolute maximum is \(\boxed{45\text{ at }x=-3}\), and the absolute minimum is \(\boxed{-4\text{ at }x=\pm\sqrt2}\).
Verify Rolle's Theorem for \(f(x)=\sin x\) on \([0,\pi]\).
The function is continuous on \([0,\pi]\), differentiable inside, and \(f(0)=f(\pi)=0\). Since \(f'(x)=\cos x\), Rolle's point satisfies \(\cos c=0\), so \(\boxed{c=\pi/2}\).
Apply the Mean Value Theorem to \(f(x)=\sqrt x\) on \([1,4]\).
The secant slope is \((2-1)/(4-1)=1/3\). Solve \(f'(c)=1/(2\sqrt c)=1/3\), obtaining \(\boxed{c=9/4}\), which lies in \((1,4)\).
Analyze increasing and decreasing intervals of \(x^4-4x^3\).

\(f'(x)=4x^2(x-3)\). The function decreases on \(\boxed{(-\infty,3)}\) (with a stationary non-extremum at 0) and increases on \(\boxed{(3,\infty)}\). Thus \(x=3\) is a local minimum and \(x=0\) is not an extremum.
Classify all critical points of \(x^4-4x^2\).
\(f'(x)=4x(x^2-2)\). Sign changes show local minima at \(\boxed{x=\pm\sqrt2}\), each with value \(-4\), and a local maximum at \(\boxed{x=0}\) with value 0.
Find concavity and inflection points of \(x^3-6x^2+9x\).
\(f''(x)=6x-12\). The curve is concave down on \(\boxed{(-\infty,2)}\), concave up on \(\boxed{(2,\infty)}\), and has an inflection point at \(\boxed{(2,2)}\).
Perform a complete curve analysis of \((x^2-1)/(x^2+1)\).

For \(f=(x^2-1)/(x^2+1)\), the domain is all real numbers; the graph is even, has x-intercepts \(\pm1\), y-intercept \(-1\), and horizontal asymptote \(y=1\). Since \(f'=4x/(x^2+1)^2\), it decreases for \(x<0\), increases for \(x>0\), and has an absolute minimum \((0,-1)\). Since \(f''=4(1-3x^2)/(x^2+1)^3\), inflection points are \(\boxed{(\pm1/\sqrt3,-1/2)}\); it is concave up between them and down outside.
Explain why \(f''(c)=0\) is not sufficient for an inflection point.
The equation \(f''(c)=0\) only makes \(c\) a candidate. Concavity must actually change. For \(f(x)=x^4\), \(f''(0)=0\), but \(f''(x)=12x^2\ge0\) on both sides, so 0 is not an inflection point.

nodes.text: An optimization problem begins as a story with several quantities and ends as a one-variable function on a feasible domain. The derivative is usually the easy middle step. The intellectual work lies in choosing variables, expressing the constraint, and deciding what the objective actually measures.
Write the domain before differentiating. Physical dimensions, budget limits, and nonnegative quantities may exclude algebraic critical points that look perfectly respectable on paper.
Optimization asks for the largest or smallest possible value of a quantity under stated constraints. The calculus is often brief. The difficult part is building the right function.

children.text: Optimization requires an objective, a constraint, a one-variable model, a feasible domain, critical numbers, endpoints, and an interpretation. A derivative locates candidates; comparison and context determine the answer.
Find the rectangle of maximum area with perimeter \(60\).
Let sides be \(x,y\). The constraint \(2x+2y=60\) gives \(y=30-x\), so \(A=x(30-x)\) on \([0,30]\). Since \(A'=30-2x\), the maximum occurs at \(\boxed{x=y=15}\), with area \(225\).
A farmer has \(600\) m of fencing for three sides of a rectangle beside a river. Maximize area.

Let \(x\) be each perpendicular side and \(y\) the river-parallel side. Then \(2x+y=600\), so \(A=x(600-2x)\). The critical point is \(x=150\), giving \(\boxed{150\text{ m by }300\text{ m}}\) and maximum area \(45{,}000\text{ m}^2\).

For fixed \(V=\pi r^2h\), use \(h=V/(\pi r^2)\) in \(S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh\). Differentiation gives the minimum condition \(\boxed{h=2r}\): height equals diameter.

nodes.text: L'Hopital's Rule and Indeterminate Forms
A Derivative Tool for Certain Limits

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] In \emph{L'Hopital's Rule}, distinguish differentiating a quotient from applying L'Hopital's Rule to a quotient limit. The quotient rule finds the derivative of one function. L'Hopital compares the limit of a ratio with the limit of a ratio of derivatives under specific hypotheses. The numerator and denominator are not being canceled.

Repeated use is justified only when the new quotient remains indeterminate. Stop as soon as the limit is determined. Excess differentiation can turn a simple answer into unnecessary algebra and conceal whether the theorem was ever applicable.

nodes.title: L'Hopital's Rule compares rates when direct substitution gives an indeterminate quotient

children.text: [title={L'Hopital's Rule compares rates when direct substitution gives an indeterminate quotient}] The forms \(0/0\) and \(\infty/\infty\) do not determine a limit because numerator and denominator may approach their targets at different rates. L'Hopital's Rule replaces the original functions by their derivatives under specific hypotheses, allowing those rates to be compared.
The rule is not cancellation and does not apply to every fraction. Identify the indeterminate form first, differentiate numerator and denominator separately, and then reevaluate the limit.

nodes.text: L'Hopital's Rule compares the local rates of numerator and denominator when direct substitution produces the indeterminate forms \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\). It is a theorem with hypotheses, not a universal permission slip to differentiate fractions.
Before using it, identify the form explicitly. Factoring, rationalizing, standard limits, or dominant-term analysis may be shorter and more informative.

Substitute first and write the form explicitly. If the form is eligible, differentiate numerator and denominator separately and re-evaluate the new limit. If it is not, use algebra, a trigonometric identity, comparison, or a transformation that creates an eligible quotient.

The equality is between limits under hypotheses, not between the original functions. Writing the limit symbol on every line helps preserve that distinction.

nodes.text: L'Hopital's Rule compares the limiting behavior of two changing quantities through their derivative ratio. It does not simplify a quotient as an algebraic identity. Away from the limit, the functions \(f/g\) and \(f'/g'\) can be completely different.

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] The central discipline in \emph{Repeated L'Hopital Applications} is form identification. nodes.text: The Rule Has a Narrow Doorway

children.text: [title={Before the formulas}] In \emph{When Not to Use L'Hopital's Rule}, distinguish differentiating a quotient from applying L'Hopital's Rule to a quotient limit. The quotient rule finds the derivative of one function. L'Hopital compares the limit of a ratio with the limit of a ratio of derivatives under specific hypotheses. The numerator and denominator are not being canceled.

Repeated use is justified only when the new quotient remains indeterminate. Stop as soon as the limit is determined. Excess differentiation can turn a simple answer into unnecessary algebra and conceal whether the theorem was ever applicable.

nodes.title: Use the simplest method that exposes the limit

children.text: [title={Use the simplest method that exposes the limit}] Direct substitution, factoring, rationalization, dominant-term analysis, and standard limits often solve a problem with less work and more insight. L'Hopital's Rule should not replace the ability to recognize those structures.
It also cannot be used when the required hypotheses fail or when the form is not indeterminate. A finite nonzero number over zero has definite one-sided behavior, not a license to differentiate.

nodes.text: A powerful method is most useful when you know its boundaries. L'Hopital's Rule does not apply to ordinary finite quotients, does not justify differentiating numerator and denominator algebraically, and may obscure a simpler cancellation or standard limit.
On exams, state the indeterminate form before invoking the rule. That one line demonstrates that you checked the theorem's doorway instead of charging through the nearest fraction bar.
Do not use L'Hopital when:

\item substitution gives an ordinary finite value; \item the expression is not a quotient and has not been transformed; \item the form is \(0/\infty\), nonzero over zero, or another determinate form; \item differentiability hypotheses fail; \item algebra, a standard limit, or dominant-term analysis is clearer.

children.text: [title={Diagnose four limits}] Decide whether L'Hopital's Rule is immediately valid.

(a) No; direct substitution gives \(1/2\). (b) Yes, form \(0/0\), though the fundamental trig limit is more foundational. (c) Yes, form \(\infty/\infty\). (d) Not immediately; transform the product into a quotient first.

A valid L'Hopital solution should explicitly identify the indeterminate form. Writing ``by L'Hopital'' over a quotient with no form check is incomplete reasoning even when the final number happens to be correct.

nodes.text: Review

children.text: Use L'Hopital only for \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\) quotients after verifying hypotheses. Recheck the form after each application. Transform products, differences, and powers before using the rule.
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}(e^{2x}-1)/x\).
The form is \(0/0\). One valid application gives \(\lim 2e^{2x}/1=\boxed{2}\).
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}(\sin x-x)/x^3\).
The form remains \(0/0\) through three differentiations: \((\sin x-x)/x^3\to(\cos x-1)/(3x^2)\to-\sin x/(6x)\to-\cos x/6\). The limit is \(\boxed{-1/6}\).
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to\infty}x^5/e^x\).
Repeated differentiation, or exponential growth dominance, gives \(\boxed{0}\).
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to\infty}\ln x/\sqrt{x}\).
The form is \(\infty/\infty\). Differentiating gives \((1/x)/(1/(2\sqrt x))=2/\sqrt x\to\boxed{0}\).
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0^+}x^2\ln x\).
Rewrite as \(\ln x/(1/x^2)\). L'Hopital gives \((1/x)/(-2/x^3)=-x^2/2\to\boxed{0}\).
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to\infty}(\sqrt{x^2+x}-x)\) and compare rationalization with L'Hopital.
Rationalization gives \(x/[\sqrt{x^2+x}+x]=1/[\sqrt{1+1/x}+1]\to\boxed{1/2}\). L'Hopital also works after verifying the original \(\infty-\infty\) expression has first been transformed.
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0^+}x^x\).
Let \(y=x^x\). Then \(\ln y=x\ln x\to0\), so \(y\to e^0=\boxed{1}\).
Explain why L'Hopital is invalid for \(\lim_{x\to0}(2+x)/(3-x)\).
Direct substitution gives \(2/3\), not \(0/0\) or \(\infty/\infty\). Therefore L'Hopital's Rule is invalid and unnecessary; the limit is \(\boxed{2/3}\).

nodes.text: Modeling Studios: Derivatives in Strong Applications
How to Read a Model Critically

A mathematical model is a deliberately simplified relationship. A derivative can analyze the model exactly while the model itself remains approximate. Good applied work therefore has two kinds of correctness: the calculus must be valid, and the model must be reasonable for the situation and range being studied.
Before trusting an answer, ask:

\item Are the units consistent? \item Is the requested input inside the model's meaningful domain? \item Does the sign agree with the situation? \item Is the magnitude plausible? \item Which assumptions could make the conclusion unreliable?

A differentiable function is convex on an interval when its graph lies below every chord, or equivalently when every tangent line lies below the graph:
If \(f''\ge0\), the derivative is increasing, which leads to this tangent inequality.

children.text: [title={A theorem is not an algebraic identity}] Cauchy's theorem explains why derivative ratios control a quotient limit. It does not say \(f/g=f'/g'\) pointwise. The intermediate point and limiting argument are essential.

nodes.text: Where Correct Derivatives Still Produce Wrong Answers

\item \textbf{Using the wrong independent variable.} State what changes with respect to what. \item \textbf{Substituting a snapshot before differentiating a related-rate equation.} Differentiate the general relationship first. \item \textbf{Treating positive acceleration as speeding up.} Compare the signs of velocity and acceleration. \item \textbf{Calling every critical number an extremum.} Verify with signs, values, or concavity. \item \textbf{Ignoring endpoints in closed-interval problems.} Absolute extrema require endpoint evaluation. \item \textbf{Calling \(f''=0\) an inflection point automatically.} Concavity must actually change. \item \textbf{Optimizing an expression before reducing to one variable.} Use the constraint. \item \textbf{Ignoring the feasible domain.} Negative dimensions and impossible production levels are algebraic outputs, not valid designs. \item \textbf{Applying L'Hopital before checking the form.} Substitute first. \item \textbf{Accepting a calculator or iteration without verification.} Check the result in the original model and inspect convergence.

nodes.text: Cumulative Practice Set
Part A: Interpretation and motion

children.text: Interpret \(R'(200)=45\) and \(R''(200)=-0.3\) if \(R\) is revenue in dollars and \(q\) is units.

Near 200 units, \(R'(200)=45\) means revenue is increasing by about \(\boxed{\$45}\) for one additional unit. \(R''(200)=-0.3\) means marginal revenue is decreasing by about \(\boxed{\$0.30\text{ per item per item}}\).
For \(s(t)=t^3-6t^2+9t\) on \([0,5]\), find velocity, acceleration, rest times, direction intervals, and speeding-up intervals.

\(v=3(t-1)(t-3)\), \(a=6(t-2)\), and rest occurs at \(t=1,3\). Motion is positive on \((0,1)\cup(3,5)\) and negative on \((1,3)\). Speed increases where \(v,a\) share a sign: \(\boxed{(1,2)\cup(3,5)}\).
Sketch a position graph whose velocity is positive and decreasing.
One example is \(s(t)=1-e^{-t}\) for \(t\ge0\). Its velocity \(e^{-t}\) is positive and decreasing, so the position graph rises while bending downward.
Estimate first and second derivatives at a central table entry using equally spaced data.

For equally spaced inputs \(x_{i-1},x_i,x_{i+1}\) with spacing \(h\), use \(\boxed{f'(x_i)\approx[f_{i+1}-f_{i-1}]/(2h)}\) and \(\boxed{f''(x_i)\approx[f_{i+1}-2f_i+f_{i-1}]/h^2}\). Include the input and output units.
A Ferris-wheel height is \(h(t)=22-18\cos(\pi t/20)\). Find vertical velocity at \(t=10\) and interpret it.
\(h'(t)=(18\pi/20)\sin(\pi t/20)\). At \(t=10\), \(\boxed{h'(10)=0.9\pi}\) height-units per time-unit, so the rider is moving upward at the wheel's maximum vertical speed.

nodes.text: Part B: Approximation, error, and Newton's method

children.text: Linearize \(\sqrt{x}\) at \(x=25\) and estimate \(\sqrt{25.4}\).
Linearize \(\ln x\) at \(x=1\) and estimate \(\ln1.03\).
At 1, \(\ln1=0\) and the slope is 1, so \(L(x)=x-1\). Thus \(\boxed{\ln1.03\approx0.03}\).
A sphere radius is measured as \(12.0\pm0.05\) cm. Estimate absolute and percentage volume error.
Use Newton's method from \(x_0=2\) to approximate \(\sqrt5\) with two iterations.
For \(x^2-5=0\), Newton gives \(x_{n+1}=(x_n+5/x_n)/2\). From 2, \(x_1=2.25\) and \(x_2=\boxed{2.236111\ldots}\), close to \(\sqrt5\).
Explain one reason Newton's method can fail even when a real root exists.
Newton can fail when the derivative is zero or nearly zero, when the start enters a cycle, or when tangents jump away from the desired root. For example, \(x^3-2x+2\) cycles \(0\leftrightarrow1\).

nodes.text: Part C: Related rates

children.text: A \(10\)-foot ladder slides away from a wall at \(1\) ft/s. Find the top rate when the bottom is \(6\) feet from the wall.
With \(x^2+y^2=100\), \(2x(1)+2yy'=0\). At \(x=6\), \(y=8\), so \(\boxed{y'=-3/4\text{ ft/s}}\): the top moves downward.
Water enters a cone of height \(15\) m and radius \(5\) m at \(3\) m\(^3\)/min. Find the water-depth rate at depth \(6\) m.
Similarity gives \(r/h=5/15=1/3\), so \(V=\pi h^3/27\). Then \(dV/dt=(\pi h^2/9)dh/dt\). At \(h=6\), \(3=4\pi dh/dt\), so \(\boxed{dh/dt=3/(4\pi)\text{ m/min}}\).
A runner passes the closest point to a camera \(40\) m away at \(8\) m/s. Find the angular rate at the closest point.

Let \(x\) be distance along the path and \(\theta\) the camera angle. From \(\tan\theta=x/40\), \(\theta'=40x'/(x^2+1600)\). At closest approach \(x=0\) and \(x'=8\), so \(\boxed{\theta'=0.2\text{ rad/s}}\).
Two vehicles are \(6\) km east and \(8\) km north of an intersection. One moves east at \(50\) km/h and the other south at \(40\) km/h. Find the separation rate.
If separation is \(z\), then \(z^2=x^2+y^2\). At \((x,y)=(6,8)\), \(z=10\), \(x'=50\), and \(y'=-40\). Thus \(z'=[6(50)+8(-40)]/10=\boxed{-2\text{ km/h}}\): separation is decreasing.
Design a related-rate problem involving an expanding sphere and solve it with units.

Example: a spherical balloon has radius \(r=3\) m increasing at \(dr/dt=0.2\) m/min. Since \(V=4\pi r^3/3\), \(dV/dt=4\pi r^2dr/dt=\boxed{7.2\pi\text{ m}^3/\text{min}}\). The model assumes a sphere and uniform radial growth.

nodes.text: Part D: Theorems and graph shape

children.text: Find absolute extrema of \(x^3-3x\) on \([-2,2]\).

Candidates are endpoints and \(f'=3(x^2-1)=0\), so \(x=-2,-1,1,2\). Values are \(-2,2,-2,2\). The absolute maximum is \(\boxed{2\text{ at }x=-1,2}\); the absolute minimum is \(\boxed{-2\text{ at }x=-2,1}\).
Verify Rolle's Theorem for \(\sin x\) on \([0,\pi]\) and find the guaranteed point.
The hypotheses hold, \(f(0)=f(\pi)=0\), and \(f'(x)=\cos x\). The guaranteed point is \(\boxed{c=\pi/2}\).
Apply the Mean Value Theorem to \(\sqrt{x}\) on \([1,4]\).
The average slope is \(1/3\). Solving \(1/(2\sqrt c)=1/3\) gives \(\boxed{c=9/4}\).
Analyze increase, decrease, local extrema, concavity, and inflection points for \(x^3-3x^2\).

For \(f=x^3-3x^2\), \(f'=3x(x-2)\): increasing on \(( -\infty,0)\cup(2,\infty)\), decreasing on \((0,2)\), local max \((0,0)\), local min \((2,-4)\). Since \(f''=6(x-1)\), it is concave down for \(x<1\), up for \(x>1\), with inflection \(\boxed{(1,-2)}\).
Perform a complete curve analysis of \((x^2+1)/(x^2-1)\).

For \(f=(x^2+1)/(x^2-1)\), the domain excludes \(\pm1\); the graph is even, has y-intercept \(-1\), no x-intercepts, vertical asymptotes \(x=\pm1\), and horizontal asymptote \(y=1\). \(f'=-4x/(x^2-1)^2\), so it increases for \(x<0\) on each domain interval and decreases for \(x>0\), with local maximum \((0,-1)\). \(f''=4(3x^2+1)/(x^2-1)^3\), so it is concave down on \((-1,1)\), up outside, and has no inflection point because \(\pm1\) are not in the domain.
Prove from the Mean Value Theorem that \(|f'(x)|\le M\) implies \(|f(b)-f(a)|\le M|b-a|\).
By the Mean Value Theorem, some \(c\) between \(a,b\) satisfies \(f(b)-f(a)=f'(c)(b-a)\). Taking absolute values gives \(|f(b)-f(a)|=|f'(c)||b-a|\le\boxed{M|b-a|}\).

nodes.text: Part E: Optimization and derivative-based limits

children.text: Maximize the area of a rectangle with perimeter \(60\).
With \(y=30-x\), area is \(A=x(30-x)\) on \([0,30]\). The maximum occurs at \(\boxed{x=y=15}\), with area \(225\).
A farmer has \(600\) m of fence for three sides of a rectangle along a river. Find maximum area dimensions.
With perpendicular sides \(x\) and river-parallel side \(y\), \(2x+y=600\). Maximizing \(A=x(600-2x)\) gives \(\boxed{x=150\text{ m},\ y=300\text{ m}}\).
Minimize surface area of a closed cylinder with fixed volume \(500\pi\).

The volume constraint gives \(h=500/r^2\). Surface area is \(S=2\pi r^2+1000\pi/r\), so \(S'=4\pi r-1000\pi/r^2=0\) gives \(r^3=250\). Thus \(\boxed{r=\sqrt[3]{250}\text{ and }h=2\sqrt[3]{250}}\), approximately 6.30 by 12.60.
Find the closest point on \(y=\sqrt{x}\) to \((3,0)\).
Minimize \(D^2=(x-3)^2+x=x^2-5x+9\), \(x\ge0\). Its derivative vanishes at \(x=5/2\), so the closest point is \(\boxed{(5/2,\sqrt{5/2})}\).
For demand \(p(q)=80-0.05q\) and cost \(C(q)=2000+20q\), maximize feasible profit.

Revenue is \(R=80q-0.05q^2\), so profit is \(P=60q-0.05q^2-2000\), with feasible demand domain \(0\le q\le1600\). Since \(P'=60-0.1q\), the maximum occurs at \(\boxed{q=600}\), with profit \(\boxed{16000}\).
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}(e^x-1-x)/x^2\).
The form is \(0/0\). Two differentiations give \(e^x/(2)\to\boxed{1/2}\).
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to\infty}x^3/e^x\).
Exponential growth dominates any fixed polynomial; three applications of L'Hopital also reduce the numerator to a constant over \(e^x\). The limit is \(\boxed{0}\).
Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0^+}x^x\).
Let \(y=x^x\). Then \(\ln y=x\ln x\to0\), so \(\boxed{y\to1}\).
Give an example where L'Hopital's Rule is unnecessary because direct substitution already works.
For example, \(\lim_{x\to0}(2+x)/(3-x)=\boxed{2/3}\) by direct substitution. The form is neither \(0/0\) nor \(\infty/\infty\), so L'Hopital is unnecessary and invalid.
